chapters.title: Chapter 4: Stress Testing and Scenario Analysis

lessons.title: Principles of Stress Testing: Beyond Statistical Models

children.text: Every method in this course so far, Historical Simulation, Parametric, Monte Carlo, Expected Shortfall, is built on the same foundation: a statistical model, calibrated on some window of data, that assigns a probability to every possible loss. Stress testing throws that foundation out on purpose. It asks a completely different question, not how likely is a bad outcome, but how bad is a specific, named, plausible scenario, regardless of what probability a model would have assigned it.
A Different Question: Not 'How Likely' But 'How Bad If'

body.caption: VaR and Expected Shortfall vs Stress Testing

cells: How much could I lose, at a stated probability?
How much would I lose, if this specific thing happens?
A statistical model calibrated on historical or simulated data
A named, constructed scenario, historical or hypothetical
Yes, built into the confidence level
Routine daily risk monitoring, position limits, regulatory capital
Answering 'are we prepared for the scenario the model says can't happen?'

children.text: Why VaR and ES Aren't Enough On Their Own

Take the Rs 50,00,000 Nifty-tracking position used throughout this course, with its 99% 1-day VaR of Rs 1,39,560. Now consider a specific scenario: Nifty falls 15% over a single week, the kind of move seen during March 2020. At 1.2% daily volatility, weekly volatility works out to roughly 2.68%, which makes a 15% weekly move a move of more than 5.5 standard deviations. Under a normal distribution, a 5.5-sigma event is, for practical purposes, treated as impossible, its probability rounds to zero. And yet it happened.

body.text: This is the whole point of stress testing. It is not that the statistical model made a math error, the model correctly says a 5.6-sigma normal event is vanishingly rare. It is that the model's own assumptions, the ones Chapter 1 flagged, normality, stable correlations, a calibration window that may not contain the worst case, were never designed to price in an event like March 2020 in the first place. Stress testing exists specifically to answer the question VaR structurally cannot: what if the thing the model says can't happen, happens anyway?

children.text: What Makes a Good Stress Scenario

body.title: A Weak Stress Test vs a Strong Stress Test

columns.label: A Weak Stress Test
points: Just scales an ordinary bad day up by a fixed multiple, 3x or 5x the daily VaR
Assumes today's correlations hold exactly, even under the shock
Assumes the position can be exited at the modeled price with no slippage
Ignores how margin requirements change once the scenario is underway

columns.label: A Strong Stress Test
points: Grounded in a genuine historical extreme or a specific, named hypothetical shock
Explicitly asks whether correlations would hold or break down under this exact scenario
Accounts for liquidity drying up, wider bid-ask spreads, and price impact when exiting
Models the margin and funding stress that accompanies a real crisis, not just the mark-to-market loss

body.title: Building a Credible Stress Scenario
steps: Define the exact risk factors being shocked, and by how much, in specific numbers
State explicitly whether correlations are assumed to hold or to break down under this scenario
Check whether the position can actually be exited at the assumed prices, or whether liquidity would dry up
Account for how margin and funding requirements change during the scenario, not just the mark-to-market loss
Compare the scenario's severity against a genuine historical extreme, not an arbitrarily scaled-up ordinary day

children.text: Stress testing is not just a quant desk exercise in India, it is a live regulatory requirement across several layers of the market. SEBI requires mutual fund houses running small cap and mid cap equity schemes to run and publicly disclose regular stress tests, including how long it would plausibly take to liquidate a meaningful portion of the portfolio under stressed, low-liquidity conditions. NSE and BSE clearing corporations run their own stress tests on the margin funds they hold, checking whether collateral would hold up if several large members defaulted simultaneously during a sharp market move, which is the same Extreme Loss Margin logic from Chapter 2 taken a step further. The Reserve Bank of India runs system-wide stress tests on bank credit, liquidity, and interest rate risk as part of its half-yearly Financial Stability Report.

body.text: Notice the common thread: every one of these regulatory stress tests asks specifically about liquidity and funding under stress, not just mark-to-market loss. A position can show a survivable loss on paper and still be genuinely dangerous if it cannot actually be sold, or if the margin call it triggers cannot be met, at the moment the scenario is playing out.

children.text: Reverse Stress Testing: Starting From the Answer

Every scenario covered so far starts with a shock and asks what it costs. Reverse stress testing flips the order: start with an outcome you consider unacceptable, wiped-out capital, a breached risk limit, a forced liquidation, and work backward to ask what combination of market moves would actually cause it. This is deliberately designed to surface blind spots a forward scenario builder might never think to construct, because it forces you to search for the scenario rather than assume you already know its shape.

body.title: Working Backward from a Breach
body.scenario: A prop desk's risk committee sets a hard rule: if the firm's capital ever falls by more than 25% in a single month, trading is halted and the book is unwound. The desk currently runs a leveraged, delta-hedged Bank Nifty options strategy alongside a Nifty futures hedge, with correlations between the two assumed to hold as they have for the past two years.
body.prompt: Using reverse stress testing logic, what would you try to identify first, and why might the delta-hedged options book be a more interesting starting point than the futures position?
body.modelAnswer: Start by asking what combination of events could plausibly wipe out 25% of capital in a month, then work backward to find it, rather than starting from an assumed shock size and checking if it is survivable. The options book is the more interesting starting point because a delta hedge only protects against small, gradual moves, it does not protect against gamma risk during a large, fast move, and it does not protect against the assumed correlation between the options book and the futures hedge breaking down exactly when both need to move together to offset each other. A credible reverse stress scenario here would specifically combine a large, fast Bank Nifty move with a correlation breakdown between the two positions, precisely the kind of scenario a model trained on two calm years would never generate on its own.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: What is the single biggest structural difference between a VaR figure and a stress test result?
options: VaR is always a larger number than a stress test result
A stress test result comes with an attached probability, while VaR does not
VaR is tied to a stated confidence level and probability, while a stress test deliberately assigns no probability to its scenario
Stress tests can only be run on equity portfolios, not derivatives
body.explanation: VaR is fundamentally a probability statement, calibrated to a confidence level. A stress test is a 'what if this happens' exercise with no probability attached, which is exactly what lets it explore scenarios a probability-based model would never surface on its own.

body.text: A statistical model can only imagine what its calibration data allows it to imagine. Stress testing exists to ask about everything else, on purpose, without needing a probability to justify asking.

points: Stress testing deliberately asks 'how bad if' rather than 'how likely', with no probability attached to the scenario, which is exactly what lets it explore territory VaR and ES structurally cannot see.

A 15% weekly Nifty drop is roughly a 5.6-sigma event under a normal model, essentially impossible on paper, yet it happened in March 2020, which is precisely why stress testing exists as a separate discipline.

A credible stress scenario explicitly addresses whether correlations hold or break down, whether the position can actually be exited under stress, and how margin and funding requirements shift, not just the headline mark-to-market loss.

SEBI's mutual fund stress testing mandate, exchange clearing corporation margin stress tests, and RBI's bank stress testing framework all share a focus on liquidity and funding under stress, not just paper losses.

Reverse stress testing starts from an unacceptable outcome and works backward to find the scenario that causes it, which is often better at surfacing genuine blind spots than starting from an assumed shock and checking if it survives.
